 The 2027 'Trump Bump' to Your Social Security COLA Is Now Official - Here's the Final Number
 How tariffs and fuel costs helped determine your 2027 raise.
 By
 David Maina, CPA 
 ,
 Edited by
 Laura Hohenstein 
 Updated
 Oct. 22, 2026
 Fact checked 
 This article was subjected to a comprehensive fact-checking process. Our professional fact-checkers verify article information against primary sources, reputable publishers, and experts in the field.
 Add Us On Google

Social Security recipients are getting a 3.6% raise in 2027, and President Trump's tariffs may have helped make that increase a little bigger. As tariffs push up prices on some everyday goods, they can also contribute to the inflation used to calculate your annual Social Security raise. 
For retirees living on just Social Security , the connection is particularly frustrating because the higher prices that helped produce a bigger raise are already taking more money out of their monthly checks. 
So while the increase is good news, understanding what helped drive it can give you a better idea of how much you'll actually benefit.

 How tariffs may affect the 2027 Social Security COLA 
Research from the New York Federal Reserve estimated that tariffs would leave consumer goods prices about 2% higher by August 2026 than they would have been without them. 
But that doesn't mean tariffs added 2 percentage points to your 3.6% raise. The research measures their effect on goods prices, while Social Security's COLA is based on a wider range of consumer expenses. 
So while tariffs may have made the 2027 raise slightly larger, there's no verified estimate of exactly how much they added or what the final COLA would have been without them.

 Why tariffs may have a limited impact on the 2027 Social Security COLA
Social Security calculates your annual raise by comparing average consumer prices from July through September with prices during the same period a year earlier. For the 2027 COLA , that means looking at how much prices increased between 2025 and 2026. 
Since Trump's tariffs were already affecting prices in 2025, some of that extra cost was included in the starting point. Yale's Budget Lab cited research estimating that tariffs had added about 0.7 percentage points to overall consumer prices by September 2025. 
Only the additional inflation caused by tariffs over the following year would have pushed the 2027 COLA higher, helping explain why their contribution to the raise may be smaller than their overall effect on prices. 
 How rising gas prices contributed to the 2027 Social Security COLA 
Earlier in 2026, the Social Security COLA was projected to be around 3.2%, but rising gasoline prices helped push the final figure to 3.6%. Gas prices jumped 9.1% in September alone, which accounted for more than half of the month's overall increase in consumer prices. 
Much of that increase had little to do with Trump's tariffs , since oil and other energy products were largely exempt from the major tariffs introduced in 2025 and 2026.

 How tariffs could affect your monthly Social Security benefits in 2027
For the average retired worker, Social Security expects the 3.6% COLA to add about $75 a month in 2027. If tariffs contributed roughly 0.2 percentage points to that increase, they'd account for only about $4 more per month, or around $50 over a full year. 
Even if tariffs added as much as 0.4 percentage points, the extra money would come to roughly $8 a month for someone receiving an average retirement benefit. 
 Why the 2027 Social Security raise may not cover rising living costs
The 3.6% raise should help with everyday expenses, although much of that extra money will be making up for price increases you've already dealt with. Groceries and other essentials have been getting more expensive throughout 2025 and 2026, while your higher Social Security payments won't start arriving until January 2027. 
And depending on where your money goes each month, you might find that the raise doesn't quite cover how much your own expenses have increased. 
Social Security calculates the COLA using an inflation measure based on spending by working households, so it may not fully capture the rising healthcare and housing costs that take up a large share of many retirees' budgets. 
 How to save money and stretch your Social Security benefits in 2027
If your expenses are rising faster than your Social Security benefits, you may be able to make up some of the difference by lowering what you spend on Medicare. Open enrollment runs through December 7, and it is the one stretch of the year when you can change your Part D drug plan or Medicare Advantage plan. 
 Premiums and drug coverage vary quite a bit from one plan to the next, so a better match can lower what you spend in 2027 without touching your benefit at all. 
If you're living on a limited income, you may also qualify for assistance that could save you more through programs like: 
 Extra Help: Reduces Medicare Part D prescription drug costs for people with limited income and resources.
 Medicare Savings Programs: Can help pay your Part B premium and, depending on the program, other Medicare costs.
 SNAP: Provides monthly food assistance to eligible households, including retirees.
A good place to start is your State Health Insurance Assistance Program, known as SHIP, which offers free one-on-one Medicare counseling, or your local Area Agency on Aging. A short call can tell you whether any of these fit your situation, and the ones that do often put more back in your budget each month than a cost-of-living adjustment would. 
 Retirement News: Almost 80% of Americans fear a retirement age increase — here’s the real reason why 
 Bottom line
The 2027 Social Security raise is good news for retirees, even if some of the higher prices behind it have already taken a toll on their budgets. What counts now is how much of that increase will actually help with your expenses. 
Once you receive your updated benefit amount, you can factor it into your retirement plan and make any adjustments needed for the year ahead. The extra money may not cover every rising cost, but it should help make your monthly budget a little easier to balance.
